aliases: Feng Huang Dancong Dong Fang Hong
Dongfang Hong (The East is Red) Dan Cong
Lao Cong Dong Fang Hong Dancong
processing: Typical of Fenghuang Dancong: sun-withered, shaken and rested to partial oxidation, fired, rolled and dried or lightly roasted.
harvest_season: As with most Fenghuang Dancong, spring is the main picking; sellers list it by harvest year.
appearance_dry: Typically long, tight, dark brown strips, as with other Dancong.
appearance_liquor: Typically clear golden to orange-yellow, as with other Dancong.
appearance_wet: Typically long leaves, green with reddened edges, as with other Dancong.
taste_profile: One commercial listing that treats it as an alias of Song Zhong describes a strong gardenia aroma. Otherwise little is documented on this tea's own cup.

brewing.notes: As with other Dancong, keep the leaf load modest and pour off quickly.

vintage_note: Specialist sellers list it by harvest year as a Chaozhou Dancong, for example as a 2026 lot. As is usual for the class, it is sold from the most recent spring, sometimes with extra months of rest after roasting.
description:
Dong Fang Hong, 'The East Is Red', is a Fenghuang Dancong sold under that name by specialist tea shops. Its exact identity is less settled than the confident name suggests.

One Chinese commercial listing gives Dong Fang Hong as another name for Song Zhong, along with Tuan Shu Ye and Da Ye Xiang, and places it in the gardenia (huangzhi) aroma group. Other accounts of that group do not list it under this name, so the link should be held loosely.

Processing would follow the usual Dancong path, with sun withering, shaking, firing and rolling. If the gardenia classification holds, floral aroma is the thing to look for. Brew it with short steeps, as these teas turn bitter quickly.

Ask the seller what the name refers to: a specific old tree, its offspring, or a general style. Since 'Song Zhong' carries a premium, a claim tying this tea to the old trees deserves some questions.
history: Little is reliably documented about this tea. One commercial listing treats the name as an alias of Song Zhong, a line it dates to the late Southern Song, but that account is unverified and that date is best taken as tradition. Where the name Dong Fang Hong came from is not explained in anything readily available.
